title: flowOn, buffering, backpressure
scopeHtml: Scope: how a Flow's upstream/downstream coroutines are wired, where flowOn/buffer/conflate/collectLatest/produceIn/channelFlow put channels and context switches, and how slow consumers push back. (Operators like map/debounce, StateFlow/SharedFlow, stateIn/shareIn and error operators belong to other chunks.)

notes.title: Suspension-based backpressure and strategies
notes.html:
The idea. Backpressure = what happens when the producer is faster than the consumer. Plain Flow has a very simple answer: the producer is paused (suspended) until the consumer is ready. Nobody is overwhelmed, nothing is lost, nothing queues.

Mechanism. A cold flow { emit(x) } and its collect { } run in the same coroutine; emit is a suspend call that simply calls the collector's lambda directly. So the producer cannot emit the next value until the collector finished the current one: total time is the sum of producer + consumer time per item. No buffer exists. This is unlike RxJava 1/2 Observable (no backpressure, MissingBackpressureException) and Flowable (explicit request(n)).

flow { repeat(3) { delay(100); emit(it) } }      // producer 100 ms per item
    .collect { delay(300); println(it) }         // consumer 300 ms per item
// total ~ 3 * (100 + 300) = 1200 ms (sequential, same coroutine)

Backpressure strategies (menu).

Need Tool
Slow consumer must see everything, and producer should keep working buffer(n) (queue)
Consumer only cares about the newest conflate() or collectLatest
Drop when full, keep old buffer(1, DROP_LATEST)
Drop old, keep new buffer(n, DROP_OLDEST)
Fan-out to many consumers shareIn / SharedFlow with buffer
Hard cap, never unbounded bounded buffer, Channel with capacity
Reduce the rate sample, debounce, batching (chunked-like custom)

Choose by asking: may I lose data, may I be late, may memory grow? The unbounded options (Channel.UNLIMITED, buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)) shift the problem to memory and eventually OOM.

Real examples. Room query flows are naturally paced by the UI; Kafka/socket style firehoses (WhatsApp message frames, trading ticks) need conflate or a bounded buffer so the UI does not stall or balloon.

Everyday picture. A conveyor belt that simply stops when the packer is busy (suspension), versus a belt that keeps running into a bin (buffer) or that throws away old boxes (drop).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Flow has "no backpressure": it has it by suspension.
  • Believing emit queues items.
  • Choosing UNLIMITED buffers to "make the slowness go away".

notes.title: flowOn and context preservation
notes.html:
The idea. A flow should run where the collector runs. If you need heavy work off the main thread, say it with flowOn and it moves only the part ABOVE it.

Context preservation. A flow must not secretly change which thread/dispatcher your collect runs on, and the producer's emissions must come from the collector's context. That is why withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(x) } inside flow {} crashes with IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: Emission from another coroutine is detected. The framework checks it (via SafeCollector) to protect collectors from thread surprises.

flowOn. flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) changes the context for all operators upstream of it; the downstream (including collect) stays in the collector's context. It is the right replacement for withContext inside a flow.

fun items(): Flow<Item> = flow { emit(db.readBlocking()) }   // runs on IO
        .map { parse(it) }                                  // also IO (above flowOn)
        .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
// collector on Main:
items().collect { render(it) }                              // Main

Spot-the-bug (placement).

flow { emit(readFile()) }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .map { heavyParse(it) }        // BUG: runs on the collector's thread (Main!), flowOn doesn't cover it
    .collect { show(it) }

Move .flowOn(...) after the heavy step, or use two flowOns. Production symptom: Perfetto/Systrace shows heavyParse on the main thread, jank, StrictMode violations, or ANR.

Real examples. Repositories return Flow with flowOn(ioDispatcher) (injected dispatcher, so tests can replace it, as taught in the Android "best practices for coroutines": inject dispatchers, expose main-safe suspend functions/flows). Room Flow queries already run on Room's own executors, so adding flowOn(IO) is redundant.

Everyday picture. A restaurant where the chef (upstream) cooks in the kitchen (IO) and the waiter (collector) serves in the hall (Main): the dish crosses the hatch but nobody swaps rooms.

Common interview traps.

  • Using withContext around emit inside flow {} (invariant violation).
  • Putting flowOn below the heavy operator.
  • Believing flowOn changes the collector's dispatcher.
  • Adding flowOn(IO) to Room/Retrofit-suspend flows that are already main-safe.

notes.title: flowOn internals, multiple flowOn and cost
notes.html:
The idea. flowOn is not free: when the dispatcher changes, it builds a small producer-consumer pipeline with a queue between the two coroutines.

Mechanism. flowOn(context) returns a ChannelFlowOperatorImpl. If the new context has the same dispatcher as the downstream, it is fused/ignored with no extra work. If the dispatcher differs, upstream is launched in a new coroutine in the given context, writes into an internal Channel with default capacity Channel.BUFFERED (64 items, or kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer system property), and the collector reads from that channel. That implies: (a) it runs concurrently, so the producer can be up to 64 items ahead of the consumer (an implicit buffer); (b) every item crosses a channel and a thread switch: cheaper than withContext per item but still some microseconds and an allocation; (c) with buffer() fusion the capacities merge.

Multiple flowOn. Each flowOn affects the segment above it, up to the previous flowOn:

flow { ... }                 // IO
  .map { a }                 // IO
  .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)    // segment 1: IO
  .map { b }                 // Default
  .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)   // segment 2: Default
  .collect { }               // collector's context (Main)

Two segments means two coroutines and two channels. Operators consecutive with the same context are fused and do not create extra channels.

Cost/perf optimization. Do not sprinkle flowOn after every operator (each costs a channel + switch). Group work: all blocking IO in one segment. For a few cheap items it can cost more than the work; for per-item huge counts (100k+) use batching, or keep the whole pipeline on one dispatcher. Using flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) for trivial map calls is a net loss. Measure with Perfetto or a benchmark (Macrobenchmark / measureTimeMillis).

Real examples. Image pipeline: decode on Dispatchers.Default (CPU), disk reads on IO, UI on Main: three segments but only where each is needed.

Everyday picture. Each flowOn is a hatch between kitchens with a trolley of 64 trays: useful for different kitchens, wasteful between two people at the same counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing flowOn only changes the thread (it also adds a 64-slot buffer).
  • Using many flowOns and paying channel costs for no gain.
  • Thinking the earlier flowOn is overridden by the later one (they stack by segment).
  • Expecting a flowOn with the same dispatcher to add a thread hop.

notes.title: buffer and unbounded buffer incidents
notes.html:
The idea. buffer() lets the producer run ahead on its own coroutine while the consumer is busy: they overlap in time instead of taking turns.

Mechanism. .buffer(capacity, onBufferOverflow) inserts a channel between upstream and downstream; upstream is run in a separate coroutine (same dispatcher, but concurrently). Default capacity Channel.BUFFERED = 64. Capacities: RENDEZVOUS (0, hand-off), CONFLATED (1 drop-oldest), UNLIMITED (no bound), or a number. Time gain for the earlier example: producer 100 ms, consumer 300 ms, 3 items: unbuffered 1200 ms; buffered about 100 + 3 * 300 = 1000 ms (producer overlaps with consumer). Gain is bounded by the slower side.

Unbounded buffer incident (post-incident review). A sensor/GPS/log pipeline used .buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) to "fix dropped frames". Producer 1,000 items/s versus consumer 100/s: the queue grows 900 items/s; with 1 KB each that is about 54 MB per minute and the app hits OOM in minutes (Crashlytics: OutOfMemoryError in kotlinx.coroutines.channels, LeakCanary shows no leak; heap dump shows a huge LinkedListChannel). A second symptom: latency grows, the UI shows data that is minutes old. Fix: bounded buffer with explicit policy (buffer(64, DROP_OLDEST) or conflate() for latest-only), monitor queue depth, add metrics for drops, and load-test at 10x.

Real examples. Upload progress, chat typing indicators (conflate); log shipping to a backend (bounded buffer + batch); Firebase/analytics event batching.

Everyday picture. A kitchen pass with a limited shelf: cooks can run ahead by a few plates, but an unlimited shelf in a restaurant with a slow waiter becomes a mountain of cold plates.

Common interview traps.

  • Using UNLIMITED to remove warnings.
  • Expecting buffer to speed up when the consumer is the bottleneck (it only overlaps work).
  • Believing buffer(0) equals no operator (it is RENDEZVOUS: still a separate coroutine).
  • Using buffer with a mutable shared object that the producer reuses (data race).

notes.title: conflate, collectLatest and slow collectors
notes.html:
The idea. conflate() = "if I'm busy, skip the stale ones and give me the newest when I'm free". collectLatest = "if a new one arrives while I'm still working on the old one, cancel my work and restart".

Mechanism. conflate() is buffer(CONFLATED): a 1-slot drop-oldest channel. The collector's processing is never interrupted; it just misses intermediate values. collectLatest { } cancels the running block when a new value arrives (see the Latest family). Differences:

conflate collectLatest
In-progress work finishes cancelled
Intermediate values skipped processed until superseded
Best when processing must complete, only newest matters next processing is wasted if outdated

Slow collector incident. A progress bar collector did delay(…)/heavy RecyclerView.submitList/layout work per emission while the source (download progress, scroll positions) emitted 100/s; the producer was paused by suspension, so the download itself slowed (network thread blocked by UI work) or frames dropped (jank in Perfetto: Choreographer frame deadlines missed). Fix: conflate() (or sample) so the producer is not throttled by rendering and the UI renders only the newest. Be careful: conflate on a pipeline that needs every event (payments, chat messages, state transitions in a machine) loses data. Also collectLatest with a non-cancellable commit gives half-done work.

Real examples. Download manager/ExoPlayer progress to a notification (conflate: older percentages are worthless); photo editor with a slider (collectLatest re-render); Maps camera updates (conflate).

Everyday picture. A scoreboard operator who, if three updates pile up, only writes the latest (conflate) versus one who erases the half-written number and starts over when a new score arrives (collectLatest).

Common interview traps.

  • Using conflate for data that must not be lost.
  • Using collectLatest where the work must finish (saves, analytics).
  • Not realising a slow collector throttles a plain cold producer.
  • Confusing conflate (skip values) with debounce (wait for quiet).

notes.title: produceIn and launchIn
notes.html:
The idea. Two ways to start a flow running "in the background" without writing launch { collect }.

Mechanism. flow.launchIn(scope) = scope.launch { collect() }, returns the Job. It is the idiom for onEach { }.catch { }.launchIn(viewModelScope). It does not wait. flow.produceIn(scope) starts collecting in a coroutine and returns a ReceiveChannel<T> you can read manually; the channel has the flow's buffer, so it is a hot start of a cold flow and a way to bridge into channel-based code (fan-out to workers). The producer coroutine lives in scope and is cancelled when the scope is cancelled; remember to cancel() the channel if you stop reading early, or the producer keeps suspended (a leak until the scope ends).

searchFlow.onEach { render(it) }.catch { showError(it) }.launchIn(viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope)

Gotcha: launchIn(lifecycleScope) is not lifecycle-aware (collects while stopped); use repeatOnLifecycle or flowWithLifecycle (flow.flowWithLifecycle(lifecycle, STARTED).launchIn(scope)). launchIn does not catch errors; an uncaught exception crashes via the scope's handler.

Real examples. ViewModel init blocks starting several listeners; produceIn for distributing work to a pool of workers (rare).

Everyday picture. launchIn sets an alarm that runs on its own; produceIn puts a mailbox in front of the stream that you open when you want.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting launchIn to block until the flow ends.
  • Using launchIn(lifecycleScope) thinking it stops in the background.
  • Forgetting to cancel the ReceiveChannel from produceIn.
  • Forgetting catch before launchIn.

notes.title: channelFlow
notes.html:
The idea. flow {} is single-lane: you can only emit from the same coroutine. channelFlow {} is a multi-lane road: you may launch coroutines and send from all of them concurrently.

Mechanism. channelFlow { } gives a ProducerScope with send/trySend, backed by a Channel (default buffered). It is the base of flowOn, buffer, merge, flatMapMerge. callbackFlow is a variant for callbacks and requires awaitClose { } (throws IllegalStateException if you forget it). The block completes when its body and all children finish.

fun loadAll(ids: List<Int>): Flow<Detail> = channelFlow {
    ids.forEach { id -> launch { send(api.detail(id)) } }   // concurrent sends
}   // completes when all children finish

Concurrency design trade-off. channelFlow { launch ... } gives unbounded concurrency by default (one coroutine per id!) so you must bound it (a Semaphore(8) with withPermit, or flatMapMerge(8)). Also the results arrive unordered. Compare: flatMapMerge(8) is the same thing prepackaged; hand-written channelFlow wins when you need custom coordination (two sources into one stream, partial results, fan-in with shared state). Trade-off: more power, easy to leak or overrun, and testing needs care.

Real examples. Combining Room + network "cache then network" emission in one flow; wrapping a location or Firebase listener (callbackFlow); concurrent image prefetch.

Everyday picture. A single-lane road (flow) versus a roundabout where several cars (coroutines) can enter at once (channelFlow).

Common interview traps.

  • Emitting from multiple coroutines inside flow {} (crash) instead of channelFlow.
  • Unbounded launch per element.
  • Forgetting awaitClose in callbackFlow.
  • Expecting order from concurrent sends.

notes.title: Operator fusion
notes.html:
The idea. Adjacent buffering/context operators are merged into one so you do not pay for two channels.

Mechanism. buffer, conflate, flowOn, channelFlow implement FusibleFlow. When chained, fuse() combines their settings: capacities add up for buffer(a).buffer(b) when both are positive, conflate() after buffer(n) conflates (capacity CONFLATED wins), and consecutive flowOn with the same context collapse (the contexts are merged, the inner one winning for conflicting elements). So flow.flowOn(IO).buffer(10) becomes a single channel of size 10 (rather than 64 + 10) and a single extra coroutine. Fusion explains why adding .buffer() after .flowOn() does not add another hop: it adjusts the existing channel. But if a non-fusible operator (like map) sits between them, they stay separate.

Real examples. Library authors (Room, Paging, Compose snapshotFlow users) rely on fusion so that layered operators do not add overhead; you see it in stack traces as ChannelFlowOperatorImpl, ChannelFlowTransformLatest.

Everyday picture. Two adjacent tollbooths merged into one lane with a combined queue, instead of two lines in series.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing each buffer/flowOn always creates a separate channel.
  • Thinking buffer(10).buffer(20) is always 30 (depends on the overflow policy and types; confirm in docs/source).
  • Assuming an intervening map fuses through (it does not).

notes.title: flowOn exceptions and cancellation
notes.html:
The idea. When the upstream runs in a different coroutine (because of flowOn), exceptions and cancellation must cross that boundary correctly.

Mechanism. An exception in the upstream segment is propagated through the channel to the collector and rethrown there, so catch placed below the flowOn catches it (and a catch above the flowOn catches it too, for errors before it). Cancelling the collector cancels the upstream coroutine, so finally blocks and awaitClose run. In the other direction, if the collector throws (e.g. render() crashes), the upstream coroutine is cancelled via the channel. With flowOn, the exception in a child coroutine is passed to the parent job in an exception-transparent way (the flow does not crash the whole scope; it surfaces at collect). Pitfalls: blocking code inside the upstream that never suspends delays cancellation; a swallowed CancellationException (generic catch (e: Exception) in the producer) keeps the producer running or leaves a leaked coroutine; try/finally cleanup that suspends needs withContext(NonCancellable).

Real examples. Crashlytics traces that start in DefaultDispatcher-worker-N but are rethrown at the collector site (the stack trace is "recovered" and shows both thanks to coroutines stack-trace recovery in debug builds).

Everyday picture. A message passed through a hatch: if the cook drops the pan, the waiter is told; if the customer leaves, the kitchen stops cooking.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing exceptions from a flowOn upstream crash on the IO thread silently.
  • Swallowing CancellationException.
  • Doing suspending cleanup in finally without NonCancellable.
  • Thinking catch below flowOn cannot see upstream errors.

notes.title: Firehose sources and location pipelines
notes.html:
The idea. When the source is much faster than the UI can use (sensors, sockets, GPS, market ticks), the pipeline must choose how to shed load, preserve what matters, and not hold memory.

Scale 10x scenario. A market feed goes from 100 to 1,000 ticks/s per symbol across 50 symbols. Naive: socketFlow.collect { updateUi(it) } — collector stalls, socket read loop is suspended (backpressure into TCP), connections time out. Better: read the socket in an IO coroutine (flowOn(IO)), parse and conflate per key (latest price per symbol, e.g. groupBy custom or a ConcurrentHashMap + sample(250)), update the UI at most 4 times a second, store history in batches. Add a bounded buffer(DROP_OLDEST) where drops are acceptable and metrics (dropped count, queue depth).

Location pipeline (ambiguous requirement). "Show my position on the map as fast as possible, and also record the full route." Those are two requirements: the map needs the newest location (conflate/sample), the route recorder needs every point (bounded buffer + batched Room insert). Ask the product owner. Implementation: callbackFlow from FusedLocationProviderClient, shareIn(scope, WhileSubscribed(5000), replay = 1), UI uses conflate() and the recorder buffer(256) + chunked-like batching to Room; the GPS request stops when no subscribers (battery). Uber/Ola/Google Maps-style apps separate display rate (tens of ms, interpolated) from persistence rate (seconds or distance threshold).

Real examples. Zerodha Kite/Groww price streaming; Uber driver app location uploads batched every few seconds; WhatsApp socket frame decoding.

Everyday picture. A river feeding a small bucket: you divert most of it (conflate), keep a dam with a fixed size for what must be saved (bounded buffer), and measure what overflows.

Common interview traps.

  • Using one flow with one policy for both "newest" and "every item" needs.
  • Using an unbounded buffer for firehoses.
  • Letting UI rendering speed throttle the source.
  • Forgetting to stop the upstream (GPS/socket) when no one is watching.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Plain Flow backpressure is suspension: producer and consumer alternate in one coroutine, no queue, no loss.
  • flowOn changes the context of operators ABOVE it only; never use withContext around emit inside flow {}; place flowOn after the heavy work.
  • flowOn with a different dispatcher creates a coroutine plus a 64-slot channel; multiple flowOns make segments; do not scatter them.
  • buffer overlaps producer and consumer; UNLIMITED buffers are a memory time bomb; prefer bounded buffers with a drop policy.
  • conflate skips stale values and lets work finish; collectLatest cancels outdated work; neither is safe for must-not-lose data.
  • launchIn starts a collection; produceIn exposes a ReceiveChannel; both need scope and lifecycle care.
  • channelFlow allows concurrent sends but you must bound concurrency; callbackFlow needs awaitClose.
  • Adjacent buffer/conflate/flowOn fuse into one channel; exceptions and cancellation cross flowOn boundaries, but swallowed CancellationException breaks it.
  • For firehoses and location, separate "latest for display" from "every item for storage" and measure drops.

questions.promptHtml: A plain flow { } has no buffer. If the collector is slower than the producer, what actually happens, and why is there no "MissingBackpressureException" in Flow like in RxJava?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that a cold Flow is just a suspending call chain, not a queue.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A cold Flow runs the producer and the collector in the same coroutine. emit() is a suspend function that directly calls the collector lambda and returns only when the lambda finishes. So a slow collector simply makes the producer wait; backpressure is implicit through suspension. Nothing is queued, nothing overflows, nothing is dropped. The cost is that total time is the sum of producer and collector work per item."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow { emit(x) } builds a SafeFlow. When you call collect { }, the block of flow { } is executed inside the collector's coroutine, with a FlowCollector whose emit just invokes your collect lambda. There is no thread hop, no channel.

collect() coroutine (one coroutine, one thread at a time)
  flow-block: compute item1 -> emit(item1) -> [collector lambda runs] -> returns
              compute item2 -> emit(item2) -> [collector lambda runs] -> returns

Math: 10 items, producer 100 ms/item, collector 300 ms/item. Sequential total = 10 x (100 + 300) = 4000 ms. With buffer() the two overlap: first item 100 ms, then the collector is the bottleneck: 100 + 10 x 300 = 3100 ms.

RxJava Flowable has an explicit request(n) protocol and a hot-capable Observable can overflow, hence MissingBackpressureException. In Flow, the suspension of emit is the request protocol: the producer cannot run ahead because it is literally blocked inside emit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val f = flow {
    repeat(3) { i ->
        println("produce $i")
        emit(i)          // suspends until collector body completes
    }
}
f.collect { delay(300); println("consume $it") }
// produce 0, consume 0, produce 1, consume 1, ... strictly interleaved

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking delay in the collector "runs concurrently" with the producer. It does not unless you add buffer/flowOn/conflate.
  • Assuming a hot source (callback registered inside callbackFlow) is also paced by the collector. It is not; see the buffer/channelFlow questions.
  • Believing "no backpressure exception" means "no memory risk". With buffer(UNLIMITED) you re-create the risk yourself.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a slow collector hurt a callbackFlow source? → The callback does trySend; if the channel buffer is full, trySend fails (or you picked a drop policy). Pacing is replaced by the channel's overflow policy.
  2. Does emit ever run on a different thread than collect? → Not unless flowOn (or channelFlow) introduces a channel; otherwise same coroutine, and context preservation forbids switching.
  3. How does this relate to the Flow context-preservation rule? → Because emit calls the collector directly, the collector must run in the collector's context; hence the "Flow invariant is violated" exception on foreign-context emission.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Flow supports backpressure through suspend." Senior: draws the sequential timeline, does the 4000 vs 3100 ms math, names buffer/conflate/collectLatest as the three escape hatches and states what each trades (latency, loss, cancellation).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team streamed 2k DB rows into a network upload with a plain flow and was surprised by 40 s instead of 15 s; no queue existed, so the producer idled for every upload.

questions.promptHtml: What does flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) change and what does it not change? Where in a chain should it go?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The #1 Flow misconception: people think flowOn moves the whole chain or even the collect block.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flowOn changes the context of everything upstream of it, up to the previous flowOn or the source. Everything downstream, including collect, keeps running in the collector's context. So it is a boundary, not a global switch. Place it right after the operators that need the other dispatcher, usually at the end of the data-layer chain, before the ViewModel or UI consumes it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow{ A } .map{ B } .flowOn(IO) .map{ C } .collect{ D }
 \_____ run on IO _____/          \__ run on collector's context __/

A and B run on IO. C and D run where collect was called (e.g. viewModelScope -> Main.immediate). flowOn is not withContext: it does not wrap the downstream. It only affects the context (dispatcher, CoroutineName, etc.); it never takes a Job (passing one throws IllegalArgumentException), since cancellation must stay with the collector.

Because flow is context-preserving, flowOn is the only sanctioned way to change the upstream dispatcher (besides channelFlow/flowOn fused cousins).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun users(): Flow<List<User>> =
    dao.observeAll()                       // Room: its own executor
        .map { rows -> rows.map(::toDomain) }   // CPU, goes to Default
        .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
// collector, e.g. viewModelScope on Main, only sees mapped lists

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting flowOn at the very start (before map) and expecting map to be off-main.
  • Adding .flowOn(IO) after Room/Retrofit-suspend sources that are already main-safe. Extra channel for nothing.
  • Expecting flowOn(Main) to make collect { } run on Main. The collect lambda belongs to the collector.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does flowOn make an onEach placed after it run on IO? → No, downstream of flowOn runs in the collector context.
  2. Can you pass a Job to flowOn? → No, it throws; cancellation is owned by the collector.
  3. What does it cost at runtime? → Usually a channel plus a producer coroutine; see the next question.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "flowOn changes the dispatcher upstream." Senior: states the direction rule, mentions the hidden channel, the Job restriction, and that main-safe sources need no flowOn.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: JSON mapping was written after a flowOn(IO) and ran on Main for every emission; the fix was moving a single line.

questions.promptHtml: Does flowOn always create a channel? What exactly happens under the hood when the dispatcher does and doesn't change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know Flow internals (ChannelFlow, fusion) from API memorizers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flowOn is implemented as a ChannelFlow operator. If the new context has a different dispatcher than the collector's, it launches the upstream in a producer coroutine on that dispatcher and passes items through a channel to the collector, default buffer size 64. If the dispatcher is the same, it skips the channel and collects directly in the same coroutine. So a dispatcher switch means a coroutine plus a buffered channel, and that means upstream can run ahead of downstream by up to the buffer size."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flowOn(ctx) -> ChannelFlowOperatorImpl. In collect, if newContext[ContinuationInterceptor] == collectContext[ContinuationInterceptor] it calls flowCollect directly (no channel). Otherwise ChannelFlow.collect does coroutineScope { collector.emitAll(produceImpl(this)) }: spawns a produce coroutine in the new context, and the collector coroutine receives from the channel.

Consequences:

  1. The producer now runs concurrently with the consumer; two coroutines, possibly two threads.
  2. Default capacity is Channel.BUFFERED = 64 (system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer); with SUSPEND overflow, the producer suspends when 64 items sit unconsumed.
  3. Memory: up to 64 items in flight, including big ones (bitmaps, 1 MB lists).
  4. Ordering is preserved (one channel, one consumer).
  5. Same dispatcher -> no concurrency gained, nothing allocated.
different dispatcher:  [producer on IO] --chan(64)--> [collector on Main]
same dispatcher:       [producer+collector in one coroutine, no chan]

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Same dispatcher: no channel
flow { emit(1) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Main).collect { }   // collected on Main -> fused, direct
// Different: channel + producer coroutine
flow { emit(1) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).collect { }     // collected on Main

Note: Dispatchers.Default vs Dispatchers.IO share a thread pool, and the coroutine machinery treats them as different dispatchers for this check, but resumption between them often stays on the same thread (the IO/Default optimization), so thread hop cost is low while the channel cost remains.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming flowOn is free. In a tight pipeline with 100k tiny items, channel overhead (per-item atomic ops, resume) is measurable.
  • Forgetting that flowOn effectively adds buffer(); adding .buffer() next to it is redundant (they fuse).
  • Believing items are processed one by one in lockstep after flowOn. They're not: upstream can be 64 ahead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) when the collector is already on Default? → Same interceptor, direct collect, no channel.
  2. How do you make flowOn lockstep? → .flowOn(x).buffer(0)? Fusion: explicit capacity wins over BUFFERED default, so buffer(RENDEZVOUS) after it makes the channel rendezvous.
  3. What if upstream throws? → Exception travels through the channel as a close cause and is rethrown in the collector after buffered items are delivered (see Q585).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Switches thread." Senior: knows about the producer coroutine, channel, 64 default, same-dispatcher shortcut, and that concurrency (not just thread move) is what it adds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Memory spikes in a gallery screen: flowOn buffered 64 full-size bitmaps ahead of a slow UI; capping with buffer(2) fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when a chain has two or three flowOn operators? Give an example and say which code runs where.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks mental model of "boundaries" and that contexts are applied per segment, not overwritten.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each flowOn governs the segment between itself and the previous flowOn (or the source). So with two flowOns you get two segments on two dispatchers plus the collector's, connected by channels. They don't override each other; a later flowOn never changes what an earlier one set."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow{ load }      // segment 1
 .map{ parse }    // segment 1
 .flowOn(IO)      // <- segment 1 = IO
 .map{ reduce }   // segment 2
 .flowOn(Default) // <- segment 2 = Default
 .onEach{ log }   // segment 3 = collector's context (Main)
 .collect{ ui }   // segment 3

Three coroutines, two channels: IO --64--> Default --64--> Main. Each segment's context is collectorContext + flowOnContext, applied to that segment only. Fusion: adjacent flowOns collapse into one operator. The upstream-most one keeps priority for any element it sets, so flowOn(IO).flowOn(Default) back to back runs upstream on IO and the second one governs an empty segment. Rule: the closest flowOn downstream of an operator decides its context.

Memory/latency: the pipeline now has stages able to run in parallel (a true pipeline), throughput = slowest stage; each channel holds up to 64.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
flow { emit(readChunk()) }
    .map { decode(it) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .map { transform(it) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .collect { render(it) }   // caller's context

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the last flowOn wins globally.
  • Chaining flowOn(IO).flowOn(Default) back-to-back to "set both". The second one has no operators to govern.
  • Over-segmenting. Each stage costs a coroutine, a channel and latency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many coroutines does the example create? → 3 including the collector; two producers + collector.
  2. Where does a thrown exception in segment 1 surface? → In the collector, after earlier-buffered items, passing through each channel.
  3. Can you get a true parallel pipeline this way? → Yes, stage-parallel (not item-parallel): one item per stage at once. For item parallelism use flatMapMerge or channelFlow + workers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Last one wins." Senior: segment model, cost of each boundary, and the difference between stage and item parallelism.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An import pipeline gained 35% throughput once decode (IO) and transform (Default) became separate stages; but two additional flowOns used for "safety" later added latency for no benefit.

questions.promptHtml:
Why does this crash with "Flow invariant is violated", and how do you fix it properly?

val f = flow {
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(loadFromDisk()) }
}

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common Flow runtime exception; tests understanding of context preservation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Flow requires that emit be called from the same coroutine context the collector uses. withContext changes the context, so the emit happens in a different one and Flow throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: Flow was collected in ... but emission happened in .... The fix is to do the work in withContext and emit outside it, or move the dispatcher change to flowOn, or use channelFlow/callbackFlow if you truly must emit from another coroutine."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why the rule exists: the collector lambda can touch UI state, locks, thread-confined data. If the emitter could call it from any thread, every collector would need to be thread-safe. Context preservation makes collect { } behave like ordinary sequential code and keeps exception transparency (an exception from a collector must propagate to the collector's caller, which is only reliable if the emit is in the same coroutine).

The check (SafeFlow / SafeCollector) compares the emitter's context with the collector's (ignoring Job identity details and checking for dispatcher/other elements); mismatch -> exception. It is a runtime check, no compile-time warning.

Three right fixes:

// 1. work in withContext, emit outside
flow { emit(withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { loadFromDisk() }) }

// 2. flowOn
flow { emit(loadFromDisk()) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)

// 3. if emission really originates elsewhere
channelFlow { launch(Dispatchers.IO) { send(loadFromDisk()) } }

Option 1 is the cheapest, no channel. Option 2 gives overlap between loading the next item and processing the current.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" by wrapping the whole collect in withContext; hides the problem and loses cancellation clarity.
  • Using launch { emit(x) } inside flow {}: same violation (different coroutine).
  • Catching the IllegalStateException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does withContext around the work and emit outside it still violate? → No, only the emit call site's context matters.
  2. Why is callbackFlow allowed to emit from any thread? → Because it uses a Channel (send/trySend is thread-safe) and the collector reads on its own coroutine.
  3. What other invariant exists? → Exception transparency: don't swallow downstream exceptions in try/catch around emit; and don't emit after catching one (throws a similar violation).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Use flowOn." Senior: explains why the rule exists (collector thread-safety + exception transparency), and picks among three fixes based on whether overlap is wanted.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migrated repo crashed at 0.8% of sessions on rotation only; the withContext emit path happened when a cache miss occurred.

questions.promptHtml: Explain buffer(capacity, onBufferOverflow). What does each parameter do, and what is the default capacity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you can choose a loss/latency/memory policy on purpose rather than sprinkling .buffer() hoping for speed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "buffer runs the upstream in a separate coroutine and puts a channel between it and the collector, so they overlap. capacity is the channel size: BUFFERED (default, 64 unless the system property changes it), RENDEZVOUS (0), CONFLATED, UNLIMITED or a number. onBufferOverflow says what to do when full: SUSPEND (default, producer waits), DROP_OLDEST, or DROP_LATEST. Only SUSPEND preserves every item."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Overflow When buffer is full Items lost? Typical use
SUSPEND producer waits no pipelines needing every item
DROP_OLDEST evict oldest, enqueue new yes, old "latest N" telemetry, sensors
DROP_LATEST discard the new one yes, new rate-limiting bursts, keep first

Rules (documented): non-SUSPEND policies require capacity >= 0 or BUFFERED, and imply at least a 1-element buffer (so buffer(0, DROP_OLDEST) behaves like capacity 1). buffer(CONFLATED) == conflate() == buffer(0, DROP_OLDEST) semantically. UNLIMITED + a drop policy is invalid (IllegalArgumentException); CONFLATED with explicit non-SUSPEND overflow also throws.

Timeline: producer 100 ms, collector 300 ms, 10 items, buffer(2): the producer fills the buffer, then waits on the collector; total ~ 100 + 10 x 300 = 3100 ms versus 4000 ms unbuffered. A bigger buffer does not speed things up beyond that: throughput is capped by the slowest stage; buffer size only absorbs bursts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
source
    .buffer(capacity = 16, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
    .collect { slowRender(it) }   // sees recent items, never blocks producer

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using buffer(UNLIMITED) to "make it fast": it only moves the backlog into heap; OOM instead of slowness.
  • Believing a larger buffer increases steady-state throughput.
  • Using DROP_* for data where every item matters (payments, events needing ack).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the difference between buffer(0) and no buffer? → buffer(0) still creates a channel and a producer coroutine (rendezvous), so producer/collector run in different coroutines; no buffer = same coroutine.
  2. How does buffer interact with flowOn? → They fuse into one channel (see fusion question).
  3. Sizing rule? → Burst size x item size must fit memory budget; size to absorb the typical burst, not the worst case, and pick a drop policy for the rest.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Buffer makes producer and consumer run concurrently." Senior: explains it only absorbs bursts, quantifies the speed-up bound, and treats overflow policy as a data-loss contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "performance fix" added buffer(UNLIMITED) before a slow upload; offline-heavy users hit OOM at 30k queued events.

questions.promptHtml: What does conflate() do and when is it the right tool? Is it the same as StateFlow's conflation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of lossy-but-fresh semantics and when dropping is a feature.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "conflate() is buffer(CONFLATED): a one-slot buffer where a new value overwrites the pending one. The collector is never behind by more than one item and always eventually sees the latest value, but intermediate values are skipped. It's right for state-like streams (position, progress, sensor readings) where only the freshest value matters. StateFlow conflates by design too, but it's a hot holder with equality check; conflate() just applies the policy to any cold flow."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanics: conflate() inserts a producer coroutine + channel with capacity CONFLATED. Producer never suspends on send. The collector, when ready, takes whatever is in the slot.

producer: 1 2 3 4 5 6   (fast)
collector: takes 1, busy... slot overwritten 2->3->4->5->6, takes 6
sees: 1, 6   (fewer, always latest at the end)

Guarantees: ordering preserved among delivered items; the last item is always delivered (so the UI converges to the final state). Not guaranteed: any intermediate item.

Contrast with StateFlow: StateFlow has an initial value, distinctUntilChanged semantics (equal values dropped), replay of current value to new collectors. conflate() has none of these; two equal consecutive values are both delivered if the collector is fast enough.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
progress
    .conflate()
    .collect { pct -> bar.setProgress(pct); delay(50) } // render at most ~20 fps

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Conflating events (clicks, "navigate" commands, payments). Dropped events = lost behaviour.
  • Expecting conflate() to reduce the producer's work; the producer still computes everything.
  • Using it on a flow whose consumer must see transitions (e.g. an FSM with side effects at each state).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. conflate vs buffer(1, DROP_OLDEST)? → Equivalent in effect for this purpose; conflate is the idiomatic name.
  2. Is the final value guaranteed? → Yes for a completing flow: the last item stays in the slot until taken (unless cancelled).
  3. Does conflate make a slow collector faster? → It lets the collector skip stale work, so the effective throughput for "latest state" improves; the total work per delivered item is unchanged.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Drops intermediate values." Senior: lists guarantees (last value delivered, order preserved), what it does not do (reduce producer work), and the events-vs-state boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A live-price ticker updated 200x/s; conflating before the adapter cut main-thread time from 38% to 6% and removed visible jank.

questions.promptHtml: conflate().collect { } and collectLatest { } both skip stale values. What is the actual difference, and when would you choose one over the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic "similar but not equal" question; tests whether you know what happens to in-flight work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "conflate never interrupts the collector: if it's busy with item 1, new items overwrite each other and the collector finishes item 1, then takes the newest. collectLatest cancels the running block for item 1 as soon as item 2 arrives, then starts on item 2. Choose collectLatest when old work is worthless and cancellable (render a search result, load details), and conflate when the work must finish once started (write to disk, commit a frame)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
collectLatest(action) is mapLatest(action).buffer(0).collect(). mapLatest is transformLatest, built on ChannelFlow (flowOn-like) that launches each block in a child coroutine and cancels the previous child on a new upstream value.

items:           1 ... 2 ... 3
conflate:        [work(1) ------------] [work(3) ----]     work(1) finishes
collectLatest:   [work(1) x]  [work(2) x] [work(3) ----]  1 and 2 cancelled

Implications:

  • collectLatest bodies must be cancellation-cooperative (suspending, ensureActive). A blocking CPU loop is not cancelled until it checks.
  • Side effects in the block can be half-done at cancellation: use try/finally/NonCancellable for must-finish cleanup.
  • With collectLatest nothing is lost because all items arrive; the older ones are cancelled work, not dropped data.
  • conflate drops values the collector never saw.

Combined: .conflate().collectLatest { } is rarely needed; collectLatest already has buffer(0) semantics.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
queryFlow.collectLatest { q ->
    val results = api.search(q)   // cancelled if a new q arrives
    adapter.submit(results)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using collectLatest for work with irreversible side effects (POSTs) and then seeing duplicate/aborted writes.
  • Assuming collectLatest cancels non-suspending code.
  • Confusing it with debounce: debounce delays upstream; collectLatest cancels downstream.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does collectLatest drop upstream values? → No; the producer is not slowed, every value triggers the block, older blocks get cancelled.
  2. What happens to an in-flight network call? → Cancelled via coroutine cancellation (OkHttp call cancelled in Retrofit suspend/Call adapter).
  3. How do you protect a critical section? → withContext(NonCancellable) { } for the commit part, or use conflate + collect.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "collectLatest cancels the previous." Senior: contrasts value dropping vs work cancelling, mentions cooperative cancellation, NonCancellable, and side-effect idempotence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A form autosave used collectLatest; slow networks cancelled almost every save, so nothing persisted; switching to conflate().collect fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: Compare the options for dealing with a producer faster than its consumer in Flow: suspend, buffer, drop, conflate, collectLatest. How do you choose, and how does this differ from RxJava?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior must turn "slow consumer" into an explicit data-loss/latency/memory decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Default is suspension: lossless, no memory growth, but producer throughput equals consumer. Buffer decouples but moves the problem into memory. Drop policies and conflate trade completeness for freshness and bounded memory. collectLatest trades work for freshness. I choose by asking: must every item be processed, may old items be skipped, may in-flight work be cancelled, how big can the backlog get. RxJava needs explicit onBackpressureXXX operators because its protocol is request(n) based and Observable has none; Flow's suspend gives lossless pacing by default."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Need Choice Memory Loss Notes
Every item, producer can wait default O(1) none cold sources only
Every item, bursty, bounded buffer(n) SUSPEND O(n) none producer pauses when full
Latest state only conflate() O(1) intermediates UI state, sensors
Latest N buffer(n, DROP_OLDEST) O(n) oldest rolling window
Keep first, ignore bursts buffer(n, DROP_LATEST) O(n) newest rate-limit
Latest, abort old work collectLatest O(1) work, not data search/detail
Unbounded UNLIMITED O(backlog) none OOM risk, only with proven bounds

Hot sources are different: you cannot make a sensor "wait". Their bridge (callbackFlow) must pick a policy at the channel (trySend result + buffer). SharedFlow has extraBufferCapacity/onBufferOverflow (see the SharedFlow chunk).

Measuring: pick capacity from rate x worst stall. E.g. 50 Hz sensor, collector stalled up to 2 s -> 100 items; at 40 bytes each = 4 KB, trivial; at 2 MB camera frames = 200 MB, not trivial -> use DROP_OLDEST with 2-3 frames.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// lossless, bounded burst absorption
events.buffer(256, BufferOverflow.SUSPEND).collect(::persist)
// freshest only
location.conflate().collect(::drawMarker)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing by habit (conflate everywhere), dropping events that mattered.
  • Forgetting a lossless buffer only delays the stall to the producer; if the producer is a callback it can't be suspended and would block/lose.
  • No metrics on drops.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Hot callback source with a lossless requirement? → Need a bounded queue and either persistent spill (DB) or backpressure to the source (ack/pull API); in-memory UNLIMITED is not a design.
  2. How do you observe drops? → onBufferOverflow has no callback; wrap with a counting channelFlow/trySend returning failure, or count emitted vs collected.
  3. Where does Flow backpressure break down? → At boundaries with push APIs: callbacks, Android sensors, WebSockets, BroadcastReceivers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: lists operators. Senior: decision table by loss/memory/cancellation, quantifies buffer size from rate x stall, treats push sources separately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat client mixed lossless typing events with conflated presence updates; both were originally conflated, and messages were silently skipped under load.

questions.promptHtml: What do launchIn, produceIn and onEach { }.launchIn(scope) do, and why would you ever use produceIn?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know how a Flow becomes a running coroutine or a Channel, and the scope/lifetime implications.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "launchIn(scope) is scope.launch { collect() }: it starts collecting in that scope and returns the Job. produceIn(scope) collects the flow in a new coroutine in scope and exposes the items as a ReceiveChannel; it's how you convert a cold flow into a channel for select, fan-out to multiple workers, or manual receive loops. In both, the lifetime is the scope's, so cancel the job/channel or the scope."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• launchIn: terminal, non-suspending, returns Job. Pattern: flow.onEach { }.launchIn(viewModelScope). Exceptions from upstream not handled with catch go to the scope's exception handling (crash for root viewModelScope launch without handler).
  • produceIn(scope): uses ChannelFlow internals; the channel capacity is that of the preceding buffer/flowOn (default BUFFERED if none). It starts the producer eagerly in scope (start = ATOMIC-like for producer). The returned channel closes on completion or closes with cause on failure. You must consume or cancel it; otherwise a suspended producer lives until scope ends.
  • Flow -> ReceiveChannel -> multiple consumers = fan-out (each item to exactly one consumer), which a plain Flow collect cannot do (each collector gets all items since cold flows re-run).
flow --produceIn(scope)--> ReceiveChannel --> worker1
                                         \--> worker2   (each item goes to one)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ch = tasks.buffer(32).produceIn(scope)
repeat(4) { id -> scope.launch { for (t in ch) handle(id, t) } }
// stop: ch.cancel()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling launchIn inside suspend code and assuming it waits. It returns immediately.
  • Using launchIn(lifecycleScope) on Android for UI collection without repeatOnLifecycle: keeps collecting in the background.
  • Leaking produceIn channels created on a long-lived scope.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. produceIn vs shareIn? → produceIn gives point-to-point (each item to one consumer); shareIn gives broadcast to all subscribers.
  2. Difference between collect and launchIn(scope) for exception propagation? → collect throws into the caller; launchIn throws into the launched Job/scope.
  3. Is the produced channel cancelled when the flow completes? → It is closed (consumers drain remaining items); cancel only needed for early exit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "launchIn is a shortcut." Senior: also reaches for produceIn for work distribution and knows lifecycle/exception consequences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upload queue exposed as Flow was collected by 4 workers directly; every worker uploaded every file (4x traffic). produceIn fan-out fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use channelFlow instead of flow { }? What does it let you do, what are its default buffering semantics, and how is it different from callbackFlow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes whether you can write concurrent producers while respecting Flow's context rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flow { } must emit sequentially from one coroutine. channelFlow { } gives you a ProducerScope: you can launch several child coroutines, on any dispatcher, each calling send (thread-safe), and the flow completes when the block and all its children finish. It is backed by a buffered channel (default 64). callbackFlow is the same builder specialised for callback APIs; it additionally requires awaitClose { } and fails with IllegalStateException if the block returns without it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
channelFlow { launch(IO){ send(a) }  launch(Default){ send(b) } }
   ProducerScope (is a CoroutineScope + SendChannel)
        |  child1 --send-->\
        |  child2 --send-->  [channel cap 64] --> collector (single coroutine)
  • The collector still sees items one at a time, in the order they entered the channel; across children order is non-deterministic.
  • Completion: block returns and all launched children complete -> channel closes. Contrast callbackFlow: block returns immediately (registers listener), so it needs awaitClose to keep the producer alive and unregister the callback on cancel.
  • Exceptions: a child failure cancels the producer scope and the exception reaches the collector.
  • Because the collector runs separately, emission context rules don't bite: sending from another dispatcher is legal.
  • Use send (suspends when full) in coroutines; trySend in non-suspending callbacks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun fetchAll(ids: List<Int>): Flow<Item> = channelFlow {
    val gate = Semaphore(4)
    ids.forEach { id ->
        launch {
            gate.withPermit { send(api.item(id)) }   // 4 parallel, arrival order
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting a channelFlow with no children completes immediately; for listener APIs use callbackFlow + awaitClose.
  • Unbounded fan-out (ids.forEach { launch }) without a semaphore.
  • Assuming results come in input order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. channelFlow vs flatMapMerge? → flatMapMerge(concurrency) is the declarative form for "map each upstream item to a flow, merge N concurrently"; channelFlow is for custom shapes (workers, shared state, mixing sources).
  2. How do you keep order while parallel? → map { async { } }.awaitAll() in batches, or sequence numbers and a reorder buffer; flatMapConcat is sequential.
  3. Why does callbackFlow crash without awaitClose? → To prevent leaked listeners: the flow would close while the callback is still registered.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "channelFlow lets you emit from different coroutines." Senior: explains channel and ProducerScope, completion rules, bounded concurrency with Semaphore, ordering loss, and builder choice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard fan-out of 40 requests via unbounded channelFlow triggered rate limiting (429); a 4-permit semaphore dropped p95 from 9 s to 2.4 s.

questions.promptHtml: You write flow.flowOn(IO).buffer(10).buffer(5).conflate(). How many channels exist and what is the effective capacity? What are the fusion rules?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep-internals question; shows whether you know buffer and flowOn are not additive channels.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Adjacent channel-based operators (flowOn, buffer, conflate, channelFlow, produceIn) are fused into one channel; the documented rules: explicit capacity beats the default BUFFERED request, several explicit capacities are summed, and a non-SUSPEND overflow policy overrides everything buffering before it. So here: one channel, the conflate() last overrides the earlier buffers, effectively CONFLATED."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules (kotlinx.coroutines docs for buffer):

  1. buffer()/BUFFERED requests "some buffer" and yields to any explicit number.
  2. Explicit sizes are added: buffer(10).buffer(5) -> 15.
  3. A non-SUSPEND onBufferOverflow (conflate included) replaces all previous buffering, since a dropping buffer never suspends upstream, so an earlier buffer would never fill.
  4. flowOn(ctx) contributes its context and (unless overridden) default BUFFERED capacity.

Examples:

Chain Channels Capacity
flowOn(IO) 1 64
flowOn(IO).buffer(10) 1 10 (explicit beats default)
buffer(10).buffer(5) 1 15
buffer(10).conflate() 1 CONFLATED
buffer(10).map{}.buffer(5) 2 10 and 5 (operator in between breaks fusion)

Practical: you can pair flowOn(IO).buffer(RENDEZVOUS) to keep the dispatcher switch without the 64 read-ahead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
source
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .buffer(Channel.RENDEZVOUS)   // fused: IO producer, no read-ahead
    .collect(::render)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "64 + 10". It's 10.
  • Believing a map between two buffers is fused; only adjacent ones fuse.
  • Designing capacity from the source and forgetting the intermediate operators change it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do drop policies override earlier buffers? → Upstream is never suspended by them, so earlier capacity is unreachable.
  2. Does flowOn(Main) when collected on Main still fuse? → It runs directly, no channel; a subsequent buffer creates one.
  3. How would you verify it? → Debug unit test with produceIn capacity, or runTest with virtual time observing emission timing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "buffer adds a channel." Senior: knows fusion exists, summing and override rules, and that adjacency matters.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reviewer asked for 'a bigger buffer'; the dev added .buffer(100) after an existing .conflate() and it silently did nothing useful; unit tests with virtual time caught the behaviour.

questions.promptHtml: With flow { ... }.flowOn(IO).collect { }, what happens when (a) the upstream throws, (b) the collector throws, (c) the collector's scope is cancelled? Which items does the collector see?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the producer/channel/collector triangle and failure ordering across a flowOn boundary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Across a flowOn boundary there are two coroutines linked by a channel. (a) An upstream exception closes the channel with that cause; the collector first drains items already buffered, then the exception is rethrown from collect. (b) A collector exception cancels the producer coroutine (structured concurrency), and propagates to the caller. (c) Cancelling the collector's scope cancels the producer too; buffered unread items are discarded. So the collector can observe items followed by the exception, and in-flight upstream work is never orphaned."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ChannelFlow.collect runs coroutineScope { collector.emitAll(produceImpl(this)) }. The producer is a child of that coroutineScope:

coroutineScope (collector side)
   |-- producer (IO) --send--> channel(64) --receive--> emitAll -> collect{}
  • (a) Upstream failure: producer completes exceptionally -> channel closed with cause. emitAll receives remaining buffered elements, then receive throws the cause. catch {} placed downstream of flowOn sees it; catch {} upstream of flowOn sees it inside the producer.
  • (b) Collector failure: emitAll throws inside coroutineScope -> scope cancels children -> producer cancelled (its finally blocks run, on its dispatcher). Exception transparency preserved: the exception is the collector's, not wrapped.
  • (c) Cancellation: parent job cancel -> coroutineScope cancelled -> producer cancelled; send suspensions throw CancellationException.
  • Ordering caveat: because of read-ahead (up to 64), the producer may already have run side effects for items the collector never processes (e.g. 64 DB rows read, 10 consumed). Upstream side effects aren't transactional with downstream consumption.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
flow {
    try { repeat(1000) { emit(it) } }
    finally { println("producer cleanup on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") }
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
 .collect { if (it == 5) error("boom") }  // producer is cancelled, finally runs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• try/catch around collect expecting to catch upstream exceptions and continue; the flow is dead after the exception.
  • Assuming items buffered before an upstream failure are lost; they are delivered first.
  • Doing irreversible side effects in upstream relying on "collector consumed it".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you put catch to handle a producer error? → After the flowOn, or before it if you want to emit a fallback from within the upstream context; catch only sees upstream.
  2. Does onCompletion run on the producer or collector side? → On whichever side of the boundary it is placed.
  3. How do you stop read-ahead from over-reading? → buffer(RENDEZVOUS) after flowOn, or smaller capacity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Exceptions propagate to collect." Senior: describes ordering (drain then throw), producer cancellation, discarded buffer, read-ahead side effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A paging loader flagged 64 messages as "read" in the DB because the producer ran ahead of a collector that crashed on message 3.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app streams accelerometer data via callbackFlow registered with SensorManager at SENSOR_DELAY_GAME (~50 Hz on test devices; many mid-range devices deliver ~100 Hz). The product wants a "high accuracy" mode at 400 Hz for 10-minute workouts, on 5.2M DAU, mid-range devices (4 GB RAM). Current code:

fun accel(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow {
    val l = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { trySend(Reading(e.timestamp, e.values[0], e.values[1], e.values[2])) }
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
    }
    sm.registerListener(l, sensor, 2_500)   // 2.5 ms
    awaitClose { sm.unregisterListener(l) }
}
// ViewModel
accel().map { filter.apply(it) }.onEach { db.insert(it) }.launchIn(viewModelScope)

Beta: at 400 Hz, 8% of sessions report "freezing" after about 4 minutes, and some reports of OutOfMemoryError. Heap dump shows 70% Reading objects. At 50 Hz no issue.
questions.promptHtml: Why did it degrade, how do you make it safe at 400 Hz, and what do you decide about data loss?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add .flowOn(IO)" or "use buffer(UNLIMITED)" or "lower the sampling rate". The first doesn't fix a slow consumer, the second guarantees OOM, and the third ignores the product ask without data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must every sample be persisted (medical-grade) or is a rolling window enough? What does the UI need (live graph at 60 fps vs final report)? Is batching in DB acceptable (end-of-workout analysis can tolerate 1 s latency)? Which thread does onSensorChanged run on (default: main thread unless a Handler is given)? Battery budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-flag the 400 Hz mode off for devices with < 4 GB or a measured insert cost > 2.5 ms. Cap rate (flag to 100 Hz) while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Consumer slower than 2.5 ms/sample (single-row Room insert ~ 3-10 ms with transaction/fsync) so the channel backlog grows: callbackFlow's default channel is BUFFERED(64) with SUSPEND, so trySend fails after 64 and samples are dropped... but heap shows Readings, so something else buffers; (2) someone added .buffer(UNLIMITED) or the DB executor queue holds unbounded tasks (Room's executor queue) because each insert was dispatched, not awaited; (3) GC pressure from 400 allocations/s of Reading + FloatArray (minor); (4) main-thread callback + main-thread collector starving UI (freeze).
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump (Android Studio Profiler) to see who retains Reading: channel buffer node vs Room executor queue vs list; Perfetto trace to see main thread slices > 16 ms; log trySend().isFailure count; measure per-insert time with measureNanoTime.
  5. Root cause: Producer rate (400/s, ~2.5 ms) beats the consumer (~6 ms single insert). The DB path accumulated queued work faster than it drained; with a hot callback source Flow's suspension-backpressure cannot slow the sensor, so the surplus must live somewhere or be dropped. Here it lived in the executor queue/unbounded buffer; after ~4 min 96k samples x ~100 B object plus queue node overhead approached the heap limit.
  6. Fix: Short term: handler thread for sensor callbacks, buffer(capacity = 512, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) plus drop counter. Long term: batch (chunked/time-window) writes, process off-main.
fun accel(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow {
    val h = Handler(sensorThread.looper)               // not Main
    val l = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) {
            if (trySend(Reading(e.timestamp, e.values[0], e.values[1], e.values[2])).isFailure) drops.incrementAndGet()
        }
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
    }
    sm.registerListener(l, sensor, 2_500, h)
    awaitClose { sm.unregisterListener(l) }
}.buffer(512, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

accel()
    .map(filter::apply).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .chunkedByTime(500)               // custom operator, or use a batching channel
    .collect { batch -> db.insertAll(batch) }   // one transaction per 500 ms

Math: 400 Hz x 500 ms = 200 samples per batch; one transaction ~ 8 ms instead of 200 x 6 ms = 1.2 s. 7. Prevention: Metric sensor_dropped_samples, benchmark tests with fake sensor at 4x expected rate, memory alert for Reading retention, review rule: "every hot source gets an explicit overflow policy". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not UNLIMITED (OOM), not conflate if raw samples are the product (we'd lose FFT fidelity), not runBlocking in the callback. Dropping samples must be an explicit product decision; if lossless is required, spill to a file ring buffer instead of heap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if lossless is required? → Write samples straight into a preallocated ring buffer / append-only file from the sensor thread; Flow carries batches for processing, not each sample.
  • Why did the UI freeze, if work was off-main? → The listener was registered without a Handler so callbacks ran on Main: 400 callbacks/s plus allocation and GC.
  • SharedFlow instead of callbackFlow? → Does not change the physics; it needs the same overflow policy (DROP_OLDEST) and offers fan-out only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A health wearable companion tripled sample rate and shipped; crash-free dropped from 99.7% to 98.9% in a week. The fix was not a bigger buffer but batching writes by time window, cutting DB transactions 200x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes flowOn(IO)/unlimited buffer, no memory reasoning.
  • Hire: identifies hot-source backpressure gap, chooses bounded buffer with drop policy, batches writes.
  • Strong hire: quantifies rates and batch math, moves callbacks off Main, adds drop metrics, and frames loss as a product decision with a lossless alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
A trading-watchlist screen shows live prices for 30 symbols. WebSocket pushes ~120 messages/s through a callbackFlow. After a release adding sparkline calculation, Crashlytics shows ANR rate up from 0.15% to 0.9% on mid-range devices (Android 11-13), plus janky frames (Perfetto: 40% of frames > 16 ms). The ViewModel:

repo.prices()                      // callbackFlow, Dispatchers.Main.immediate collector
    .map { buildSparkline(it) }    // ~12 ms CPU per message
    .collect { _state.update { s -> s.with(it) } }

Logs: Skipped 87 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread. Backend team says "server is fine".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without changing the server.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in withContext(IO)" (wrong dispatcher, throws invariant violation when inside flow) or "debounce(100)" without explaining why the main thread is the issue.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does collect run (Main.immediate)? Does the UI need every tick or the latest per symbol? Is prices() a hot source with a buffer already? Does the 12 ms cost scale with list size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag sparkline off, or throttle updates to 4/s per symbol, restoring frame times within one release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) map { buildSparkline } runs on Main because there is no flowOn: 120 x 12 ms = 1.44 s of main-thread work per second, i.e. 144% of one core -> ANR; (2) _state.update triggers full list diff each message; (3) channel backlog growing since consumer < producer; (4) GC (red herring if allocation is steady).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto/System trace: Choreographer#doFrame plus the coroutine slice; main-thread CPU in Profiler; temporarily log Looper.myLooper() in map; count in-flight backlog via buffer size metrics.
  5. Root cause: The CPU-heavy map ran on the collector's dispatcher (Main) since flowOn was missing, and the consumer was 12 ms vs a 8.3 ms production interval, so the callback channel filled and each frame was starved.
  6. Fix: Move compute off main and lossy-latest at the UI edge:
repo.prices()
    .map { buildSparkline(it) }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)      // upstream of this on Default
    .conflate()                       // UI only needs the latest per frame
    .sample(250)                      // or per-symbol throttling
    .collect { _state.update { s -> s.with(it) } }

Now the work is on Default; conflate bounds the backlog; UI updates at 4/s per stream. Better: group by symbol and keep the latest per symbol, then update the state once per frame batch. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric on the watchlist; StrictMode for main-thread work; lint/review rule "heavy map must be followed by flowOn". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't launch(Dispatchers.IO) per message (unbounded concurrency, out-of-order); don't use IO for CPU work; don't increase buffer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why Default and not IO? → CPU-bound, parallelism = cores; IO is for blocking.
  • After the fix p95 frame is still 20 ms. → Check the diff/bind cost: use DiffUtil on background, Immutable list in Compose, stable keys.
  • Is conflate before or after flowOn? → After; it makes the channel between Default and Main lossy so the producer never waits on Main.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A stock-quote screen ANR'd only on "slow Fridays" when volatility tripled message rates; the system worked at 30 msg/s but collapsed at 120. Load tests now replay recorded busy sessions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network or just adds debounce.
  • Hire: spots missing flowOn, uses Default, adds conflate/sample.
  • Strong hire: does the 120x12 ms utilization math, identifies the channel backlog, adds benchmarks and per-symbol batching.

questions.contextHtml:
A code review. The goal: parse a 3 MB JSON file off the main thread and show a list; QA says the screen freezes ~900 ms on a Pixel 4a.

fun items(): Flow<List<Item>> = flow {
    val text = file.readText()                 // 3 MB
    emit(parser.parse(text))                   // 700 ms CPU
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
 .map { list -> list.sortedBy { it.name } }    // 150 ms CPU for 40k items
 .onEach { cache.put(it) }                     // ~50 ms
 .flowOn(Dispatchers.Main)
viewModelScope.launch { items().collect { _ui.value = it } }

The author says "I put flowOn at the end so everything runs on the right thread".
questions.promptHtml: What runs where, why does the screen freeze, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "flowOn(Main) at the end makes the whole thing run on Main"; or "move it to the start". Both show misunderstanding of direction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is cache.put thread-safe, does it touch UI? Is the sort needed or can the backend order it? Is the file cached across screens?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; if in production, patch with the fix below, hot-fix release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) The map and onEach are upstream of flowOn(Main) so they run on Main: 200 ms plus. (2) Parsing 700 ms is on IO, fine (red herring for freeze) but it's CPU, ideally Default. (3) collect sets _ui.value on Main.immediate; cheap.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto/Android Profiler CPU trace: main-thread slices around the coroutine; log Thread.currentThread().name in each stage.
  5. Root cause: Upstream of the first flowOn = IO (flow body). Between the two flowOns (map, onEach) = Main, because the later flowOn(Main) covers that segment. Downstream = collector (Main). A flowOn(Main) at the end made the CPU stages main-thread bound. Also, reading and CPU parsing both in IO is mixing blocking and CPU work (minor).
  6. Fix:
fun items(): Flow<List<Item>> = flow {
    val text = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { file.readText() }  // allowed: emit is outside
    emit(text)
}
    .map { parser.parse(it) }                // CPU
    .map { it.sortedBy(Item::name) }
    .onEach { cache.put(it) }                // thread-safe cache assumed
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)             // single boundary for all upstream stages

Collector remains on Main only for the _ui.value assignment. withContext(IO) inside flow {} is fine when emit happens outside it. 7. Prevention: Review rule: "flowOn goes immediately downstream of the last heavy operator; never flowOn(Main)" (collectors are already main), custom lint on flowOn(Dispatchers.Main), StrictMode, Macrobenchmark startup/scroll checks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't put withContext(Default) around collect; don't add flowOn(IO) before and after for "safety".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can flowOn(Main) ever be right? → When the collector runs elsewhere (e.g. Default) but a stage must touch a main-only API; rare, usually design smell.
  • Why not a single flowOn(IO) at the end? → CPU work would starve IO threads (64 limit shared), and IO and Default share a pool; it works but Default is semantically right.
  • Would .buffer() help the freeze? → No; the problem is where CPU runs, not overlap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catalog app had flowOn(Main.immediate) copy-pasted across 12 repositories from one snippet; one lint rule removed all of them and ANR dropped 30%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes flowOn at the end controls the whole chain.
  • Hire: segments the chain correctly and fixes with one flowOn after the heavy stages.
  • Strong hire: separates blocking IO from CPU, uses withContext inside flow legally, adds lint/benchmark prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
A home screen needs enrichments for up to 60 product IDs: each api.detail(id) takes 250-900 ms (p95 1.2 s), the backend allows at most 6 concurrent requests per client before returning 429. UX wants cards to appear as they arrive, not wait for all, and wants cancellation when the user leaves. Current sequential implementation:

flow { ids.forEach { emit(api.detail(it)) } }   // 60 x ~500 ms = 30 s total

A teammate proposes ids.map { async { api.detail(it) } }.awaitAll(); another proposes ids.asFlow().flatMapMerge { flow { emit(api.detail(it)) } }.
questions.promptHtml: Choose and implement an approach; discuss ordering, failure, memory, cancellation.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks awaitAll (all-at-once, 60 concurrent -> 429, no progressive display), or flatMapMerge with default concurrency (16) exceeding the limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does order matter for display? Should one failed detail fail the whole screen? Is 429 retried by an interceptor? Is the cache per id? Should the first paint be above the fold only (prioritize 8)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). Baseline: sequential 30 s; target < 6 s.
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked: (1) flatMapMerge(concurrency = 6): declarative, ordered by completion, built-in bounded parallelism; (2) channelFlow + Semaphore: custom control (priorities, per-item retry); (3) awaitAll: no progressive results, bursts 60; (4) sequential: too slow.
  4. How I'd verify: Fake API with virtual time (runTest) asserting max concurrent calls <= 6 and arrival order; staging load test; check 429 rate in backend dashboards.
  5. Root cause of slowness: Serial latency adds up: 60 x 500 ms. With concurrency 6: ceil(60/6) = 10 waves x ~500 ms ~ 5 s (up to ~8 s at p95).
  6. Fix:
fun details(ids: List<Int>): Flow<Result<Detail>> =
    ids.asFlow()
        .flatMapMerge(concurrency = 6) { id ->
            flow { emit(runCatching { api.detail(id) }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }) }
        }

runCatching catches CancellationException, so rethrow it; better use try/catch. For priority/retry use the channelFlow variant:

fun details(ids: List<Int>) = channelFlow {
    val gate = Semaphore(6)
    ids.forEach { id -> launch { gate.withPermit { send(api.detail(id)) } } }
}.buffer(8)
