Consumer: collect { adapter.add(it) } with buffer bounding memory (60 small objects anyway). 7. Prevention: Test max-concurrency invariant; a shared ApiConcurrencyLimiter in the HTTP layer (OkHttp Dispatcher.maxRequestsPerHost = 6) as the real guard. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not awaitAll (no progress, burst), not launch per id without a gate, not unlimited flatMapMerge. Ordering by completion means UI must key items by id; if stable order is required, use indexed results and sortedBy at insertion, or flatMapConcat for strictly sequential (slow).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One id always fails with 500; should the whole thing fail? → Wrap each in Result and emit failures as items so the screen shows partial results; catch upstream would terminate the stream.
  • User navigates away mid-flight. → Collector scope cancels; flatMapMerge/channelFlow children are cancelled; OkHttp calls are cancelled by suspend call cancellation.
  • Server now allows 12. → Concurrency is a constant/remote config; also let OkHttp dispatcher be the true cap.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rollout using unbounded async during a sale tripled backend 429s; the incident review replaced it with a per-host limit in the HTTP client plus flatMapMerge(6).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: awaitAll or sequential, no concurrency limit.
  • Hire: flatMapMerge/semaphore with 6, ordering and failure discussed.
  • Strong hire: math on waves, CancellationException handling, HTTP-layer limit, virtual-time test for max concurrency.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing driver app: FusedLocationProvider delivers updates every 1 s (drivers) via callbackFlow. Three consumers: (a) map marker (60 fps, latest only), (b) trip-distance calculator (needs every fix, in order), (c) uploader sending a batch to the server every 5 s over flaky 3G (can stall for 30+ s). PM says: "make sure it's smooth and we never lose data". Current: one shared flow collected by all three in the same coroutine via merge-like code; when uploads stall the marker freezes.
questions.promptHtml: The requirements conflict ("smooth" vs "never lose"). How do you structure the flow pipeline, buffers and loss policies?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Single buffer(UNLIMITED) and call it done; or conflate() on everything (violates distance accuracy and upload completeness).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What counts as "data" (every fix vs trip polyline at 5 s granularity)? Is the server idempotent (dedup by timestamp)? What's the max acceptable upload delay and storage cap offline? Is billing computed on server or client?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Decouple the uploader immediately so a stalled network can't pause the marker; this is a ship-now fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) consumers share one coroutine/sequential collection so the slowest dictates pace; (2) no per-consumer loss policy; (3) the upload stage holds an in-memory queue growing during stalls.
  4. How I'd verify: Network Link Conditioner / emulator throttling to simulate 30 s stalls; coroutine debug probes; logs of timestamps between fix and marker draw; memory graph during offline.
  5. Root cause: Conflated requirements: one pipeline for three semantic contracts. Different consumers need different backpressure contracts.
  6. Fix: Split by contract:
    • Fan-out hot source with a SharedFlow (see shared-flow chunk) or one collector that writes to a durable store first.
    • (a) Marker: .conflate() at the edge: freshest only.
    • (b) Distance: lossless, in-order, runs on Default; buffer(64) SUSPEND; trivial CPU.
    • (c) Upload: persist first, upload from storage: every fix appended to a Room table (WAL, batch inserts per second); an uploader reads unsent rows in batches of up to 100 and marks them on ack. Memory stays flat during any stall; "never lose" is satisfied by disk, not by a channel.
val fixes = locationFlow()               // callbackFlow, buffer(64) lossless-ish
scope.launch { fixes.collect { dao.append(it) } }                    // durable
scope.launch { fixes.conflate().collect { marker.move(it) } }        // smooth (own collector)
scope.launch { fixes.runningFold(Dist.ZERO, ::acc).collect(::show) } // exact
// uploader: poll DB, not the flow

(In real code the shared flow is obtained with shareIn.) 7. Prevention: Offline soak test, storage cap with policy (drop oldest unsent beyond 24 h but metric it), contract table in the design doc per consumer (lossless/conflated). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No unbounded RAM buffer for "never lose"; no conflate on the persisted path; no single-collector merge. Truly "never lose" has a bound: disk and process death; I'd state that to PM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process killed mid-trip. → Persisted rows survive; foreground service + WorkManager resumes upload; dedup by (tripId, timestamp).
  • Marker still janks. → CPU in the marker path: do interpolation on Default and animate with ValueAnimator; conflate before it.
  • Could you use collectLatest for the marker? → Yes if rendering is cancellable work; conflate is simpler if the draw is quick.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A courier app lost 0.3% of trip points because an in-memory queue was dropped on process death; moving to persist-first removed disputes entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one pipeline, UNLIMITED buffer.
  • Hire: separates consumers by contract, conflates marker, buffers lossless path.
  • Strong hire: persist-first with durable queue, challenges "never lose", defines bounds and dedup.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review of an OOM crash spike: 2.1% of sessions on Android Go (2 GB RAM) devices crashed within 10 minutes on the "Gallery sync" screen. Crashlytics: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 12582928 byte allocation ... free memory 7MB. Change in release 5.14: "speed up thumbnails pipeline".

photos.asFlow()                              // 4,000 local URIs
    .map { decodeThumb(it) }                 // 12 MB bitmap (4 MP ARGB_8888), 40 ms each
    .buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)               // "so decoding never waits for the UI"
    .collect { uploadAndShow(it) }           // 600 ms each on average

Heap graph: thousands of Bitmap instances retained by BufferedChannel segments. Rollback restored stability.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through the review: root cause, timeline math, fix, and process changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bitmaps are big, use Glide" (misses the buffer), or "increase largeHeap".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why was UNLIMITED chosen (a benchmark showing +20% speed)? What device classes were in the perf test? Is the UI the true bottleneck, or the upload?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rollback done; hotfix flag to disable the pipeline on devices with isLowRamDevice.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) UNLIMITED buffer; (2) bitmap leak in uploadAndShow (red herring: the heap shows retention in the channel, not UI); (3) largeHeap missing; (4) fragmentation.
  4. How I'd verify: Heap dump: path-to-GC-root from Bitmaps -> BufferedChannel -> collector; reproduce on a 2 GB emulator with 4,000 images; log channel size.
  5. Root cause (math): Producer: 40 ms per decode = 25 images/s. Consumer: 600 ms = 1.67 images/s. Backlog growth = 25 - 1.67 = 23.3 images/s x 12 MB = ~280 MB/s. A 2 GB device gives an app heap of ~192-256 MB: exhausted in under 1 second, which in practice means ~20 bitmaps; the crash appears within the first minute (the ten-minute figure includes screen navigation). Even a 4 GB device with 512 MB heap fails in ~2 s. Perf testing used 20 photos, so the buffer never became large.
  6. Fix:
photos.asFlow()
    .map { decodeThumb(it) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .buffer(2)                       // bounded: at most ~3 bitmaps in flight (36 MB)
    .collect { uploadAndShow(it) }

Better: decode into the smallest size needed (e.g. 256x256 RGB_565/ARGB_8888 = 256 KB), recycle via BitmapPool, and run uploads with concurrency 3 using flatMapMerge(3), since the real bottleneck is the 600 ms upload (3 parallel -> 200 ms/image effective). 7. Prevention: Ban UNLIMITED in review (lint: custom detector for Channel.UNLIMITED / buffer(UNLIMITED)); require "worst-case memory = capacity x item size" in the PR; perf tests with realistic data and low-RAM device in CI; memory metric in startup/benchmark suite. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: largeHeap only delays the OOM; DROP_OLDEST would silently skip uploads; unlimited Dispatchers.IO parallelism would also OOM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would buffer(2) still be bounded when decode is faster? → Yes: producer suspends when 2 are queued; in-flight at most capacity + 1 being processed + 1 being produced.
  • How about conflate? → Wrong: every photo must upload.
  • What if the product wants the UI to show decode progress ahead of upload? → Show thumbnails from a small memory-bounded cache and lazy-load; don't use the pipeline buffer for UI prefetch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The "20% faster" benchmark was real on a flagship with 50 photos; on production's low-end devices the same change was an outage. Since then perf tests ship with a "worst device" gate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames bitmaps/Glide or largeHeap.
  • Hire: identifies UNLIMITED backlog and bounds the buffer.
  • Strong hire: full rate math (25/s vs 1.67/s x 12 MB), identifies true bottleneck, adds lint/review/perf-gating process.

questions.contextHtml:
An inbox screen observes Room: dao.observeThreads(): Flow<List<ThreadEntity>> (about 5,000 rows, 1.5 KB each). A new sync writes in bursts: 30 inserts within 1 s as messages arrive. Profile on a Redmi 9 (Android 11): each Room invalidation re-queries 5,000 rows (~35 ms) and the pipeline below runs per emission; battery team reports the screen at 11% CPU while idle-syncing, and p95 time-to-render after a sync is 480 ms.

dao.observeThreads()
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)                          // added "to keep Room off main"
    .map { rows -> rows.map { it.toUi(clock, fmt) } }   // 5,000 mappings, ~60 ms
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .collect { adapter.submitList(it) }

Perf review asks to cut CPU and render latency without changing the DB schema.
questions.promptHtml: What would you change in the Flow pipeline, and what would you measure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add buffer()" or "use more dispatchers"; ignores that the work itself repeats 30 times per burst.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does UI need each intermediate state (no)? Is toUi pure and thread-safe? Can the list be diffed incrementally? Is Room's query already running on its query executor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a 50-100 ms throttle for the burst; this alone cuts the repeated 30 recomputations to 1-2.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Redundant recomputation per invalidation (30 x (35 + 60) ms ~ 2.9 s CPU per burst); (2) the first flowOn(IO) is a pointless hop: Room's Flow already queries on its own executor and is main-safe, so it adds a channel and thread switch; (3) submitList of 5,000 items diffs on a background thread but with 30 lists queued; (4) allocation pressure from 5,000 UI objects x 30.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto + Android Studio CPU profiler; log the count of emissions per burst; Debug.threadAllocCount; microbenchmark of toUi.
  5. Root cause: Each Room table-invalidation emits a fresh full list; with 30 writes in a second there are up to 30 emissions, each re-mapped fully; the extra flowOn(IO) adds overhead but isn't the main cost.
  6. Fix:
dao.observeThreads()                       // no flowOn(IO): Room handles its own threads
    .conflate()                            // drop stale lists while mapping
    .map { rows -> rows.map { it.toUi(clock, fmt) } }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)           // one boundary, fused with conflate's channel
    .collect { adapter.submitList(it) }

Careful with placement: conflate() before the map + flowOn: the channel created by flowOn is placed after the map; to make the map's input conflated you rely on fusion order: .map{...}.flowOn(Default).conflate() conflates between Default and Main; conflate().map{}.flowOn(Default) lets the mapping stage skip stale lists because the conflating channel sits ahead of the mapper. If the DB query (producer) and mapper are both fast to start, add .debounce(50) (for the burst case) at the start of the stage. Expected result: 30 emissions collapse to 2-3; CPU per burst falls from ~2.9 s to ~0.3 s (3 x 95 ms), and p95 render from 480 to ~160 ms (50 ms debounce + 35 query + 60 map + submit). Further: map only changed rows (cache UiModel by id+version) or use Paging/a smaller projection (@Query columns needed for the list). 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark CPU for sync-with-open-screen; count emissions per second as a debug metric; distinctUntilChanged() if the list content can be equal. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't debounce too high (UI feels stale: 50-100 ms is invisible; 500 ms is not); don't add flowOn(IO) to Room flows; don't use collectLatest with submitList (cancelling the submit gains nothing).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Room need no flowOn? → Room's Flow return type runs the query on its query executor (or on the collector's context for suspend queries using withContext(queryDispatcher)), so collecting on Main is allowed.
  • Debounce vs sample here? → Debounce waits for quiet (can starve under continuous writes); sample guarantees periodic updates; for sync bursts I'd use sample/conflate + trailing so the screen still updates during long syncs.
  • Would a bigger buffer help? → No, it queues stale lists; memory up, latency up.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A messaging app's idle CPU dropped 60% after replacing a "defensive" flowOn(IO) plus per-emission full mapping with conflate and id-keyed UI model caching; the Room flow itself was never the problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds buffer or more dispatchers.
  • Hire: removes redundant flowOn, dedups/conflates emissions, quantifies repeated work.
  • Strong hire: reasons about operator placement vs fusion, measures emissions per burst, avoids over-debounce and proposes incremental mapping.
